task: Compile quantitative data from administrative, institutional, or published records into datasets to characterize patterns and change over time.
substep: Identify the serial records suitable for quantification (censuses, tax rolls, parish registers, price currents, trade ledgers, court dockets, institutional reports) and assess their continuity, coverage, and comparability across the period.

task: Compile quantitative data from administrative, institutional, or published records into datasets to characterize patterns and change over time.
substep: Define the units of observation and the variables to be extracted (e.g., households, transactions, individuals, years), deciding what each row and column of the eventual dataset will represent.

task: Compile quantitative data from administrative, institutional, or published records into datasets to characterize patterns and change over time.
substep: Establish a coding scheme and standardized categories to reconcile historically variable terminology, currencies, weights, occupational labels, and administrative units into consistent, tabulable fields.

task: Compile quantitative data from administrative, institutional, or published records into datasets to characterize patterns and change over time.
substep: Transcribe figures and entries from the records into a structured spreadsheet or relational database, preserving original values alongside standardized ones and recording source citations for each entry.

task: Compile quantitative data from administrative, institutional, or published records into datasets to characterize patterns and change over time.
substep: Handle gaps, illegible entries, duplicate records, and inconsistent enumeration by flagging missing data and documenting decisions about interpolation, exclusion, or aggregation.

task: Compile quantitative data from administrative, institutional, or published records into datasets to characterize patterns and change over time.
substep: Normalize and convert values to comparable metrics across time and place (deflating prices, converting currencies and measures, adjusting for changing boundaries or reporting practices) so series can be compared.

task: Compile quantitative data from administrative, institutional, or published records into datasets to characterize patterns and change over time.
substep: Aggregate and tabulate the compiled entries into time series, cross-tabulations, and summary tables, computing rates, ratios, and totals that describe the phenomenon under study.

task: Compile quantitative data from administrative, institutional, or published records into datasets to characterize patterns and change over time.
substep: Interpret the resulting patterns and trends against the historical context, weighing whether observed change reflects real historical shifts or artifacts of the record-keeping itself.

task: Compile quantitative data from administrative, institutional, or published records into datasets to characterize patterns and change over time.
substep: Document the dataset with a codebook, source notes, and metadata detailing provenance and construction choices to make the compilation transparent and reusable.

task: Analyze linguistic forms in data to make explicit their sources, meanings, or relations to other forms
substep: Segment the data stream into the relevant units of analysis (phones, morphemes, words, phrases, clauses) so that discrete forms can be isolated for treatment.

task: Analyze linguistic forms in data to make explicit their sources, meanings, or relations to other forms
substep: Identify and label each form's grammatical category and morphosyntactic properties, assigning part-of-speech and feature tags (e.g., tense, case, number, aspect).

task: Analyze linguistic forms in data to make explicit their sources, meanings, or relations to other forms
substep: Parse morphologically complex forms into their constituent morphemes and produce an interlinear morpheme-by-morpheme gloss following Leipzig glossing conventions.

task: Analyze linguistic forms in data to make explicit their sources, meanings, or relations to other forms
substep: Determine the meaning or function of each form in context, disambiguating senses and assigning semantic/pragmatic values relative to the surrounding discourse.

task: Analyze linguistic forms in data to make explicit their sources, meanings, or relations to other forms
substep: Trace each form's source or origin—citing a lemma/dictionary headword, identifying etymology or loan status, and assigning the underlying (base) form to a surface variant.

task: Analyze linguistic forms in data to make explicit their sources, meanings, or relations to other forms
substep: Relate the form to other forms in the data—paradigmatic sets, allomorphs/allophones, cognates, derivational families, or syntactic dependencies—stating the nature of each relation.

task: Analyze linguistic forms in data to make explicit their sources, meanings, or relations to other forms
substep: Record the analysis in a structured representation (annotation tiers in ELAN/FLEx, glossed example lines, feature matrices, tree/dependency structures) with the analytic decisions made explicit.

task: Analyze linguistic forms in data to make explicit their sources, meanings, or relations to other forms
substep: Check the analysis against the rest of the dataset for internal consistency, revising labels and glosses where parallel forms reveal misanalysis.

task: Compile and curate text corpora from web sources, digitized archives, or existing linguistic databases.
substep: Define the corpus design specification: target language(s)/dialects, genres, time period, register, and estimated token/document counts, plus inclusion/exclusion criteria so sampling stays representative of the research question.

task: Compile and curate text corpora from web sources, digitized archives, or existing linguistic databases.
substep: Inventory candidate sources and check their licensing and access terms (e.g., Creative Commons on Wikipedia dumps, API terms for Twitter/Reddit, robots.txt for crawling, or DUAs for archives like HathiTrust/ELRA/LDC), recording provenance and permissions for each.

task: Compile and curate text corpora from web sources, digitized archives, or existing linguistic databases.
substep: Acquire the raw data: run a scraper with Scrapy/BeautifulSoup or use Common Crawl WET/WARC files for web text, call REST APIs for social media, download bulk dumps (Wikipedia, OpenSubtitles), or pull existing collections from LDC/ELRA/CLARIN and Hugging Face datasets.

task: Compile and curate text corpora from web sources, digitized archives, or existing linguistic databases.
substep: Extract clean text from source formats: strip HTML boilerplate with tools like trafilatura or jusText, run OCR (Tesseract/ABBYY) on scanned archive images, and convert PDF/XML/TEI into plain UTF-8 text with document structure preserved.

task: Compile and curate text corpora from web sources, digitized archives, or existing linguistic databases.
substep: Detect and filter by language using fastText lid.176 or CLD3, discarding documents below a confidence threshold or in unwanted languages, and flag code-switched segments for the mixed portion.

task: Compile and curate text corpora from web sources, digitized archives, or existing linguistic databases.
substep: Normalize encoding and typography: fix mojibake with ftfy, standardize Unicode normalization (NFC), unify quotation marks and whitespace, and — for historical or non-standard text — apply spelling normalization before further processing.

task: Compile and curate text corpora from web sources, digitized archives, or existing linguistic databases.
substep: Deduplicate at document and near-duplicate level using MinHash/LSH (e.g., datasketch) or exact hashing, and remove boilerplate/paragraph-level repeats to prevent skewed frequency counts.

task: Compile and curate text corpora from web sources, digitized archives, or existing linguistic databases.
substep: Apply quality filters: drop documents with excessive symbol-to-word ratios, too-short texts, OCR garbage, or spam/adult content using heuristic thresholds and perplexity filtering against a reference LM (following C4/Gopher-style rules).

task: Compile and curate text corpora from web sources, digitized archives, or existing linguistic databases.
substep: Attach and store metadata per document (source URL, date, author/genre, license, OCR confidence) in a structured schema so downstream users can subset by domain or time period.

task: Compile and curate text corpora from web sources, digitized archives, or existing linguistic databases.
substep: De-identify and scrub sensitive personal information (emails, phone numbers, names) where required by the DUA or ethics protocol, using regex plus NER-based PII detection.

task: Compile and curate text corpora from web sources, digitized archives, or existing linguistic databases.
substep: Segment and tokenize the cleaned text into sentences and tokens with language-appropriate tools (spaCy, Stanza, or UDPipe), keeping raw and processed versions aligned.

task: Compile and curate text corpora from web sources, digitized archives, or existing linguistic databases.
substep: Audit the resulting corpus for demographic and linguistic skew across sources and dialects, checking whether certain groups or varieties are over/under-represented before release.

task: Compile and curate text corpora from web sources, digitized archives, or existing linguistic databases.
substep: Package the corpus with a versioned release (e.g., train/dev/test splits), a datasheet/data statement documenting composition, collection process, and known limitations, and store it in a reproducible format (JSONL/CoNLL-U/HF datasets).

task: Develop and apply annotation schemes for labeling linguistic phenomena such as part-of-speech, named entities, or discourse relations.
substep: Define the target linguistic phenomenon and annotation goals precisely, e.g. deciding whether we are labeling PTB-style POS tags, CoNLL-style named entities, or PDTB-style discourse relations, and specifying the intended downstream use.

task: Develop and apply annotation schemes for labeling linguistic phenomena such as part-of-speech, named entities, or discourse relations.
substep: Ground the label inventory in relevant linguistic theory, e.g. choosing Universal Dependencies POS categories or RST/PDTB discourse frameworks, so the tagset reflects established syntactic/semantic/pragmatic distinctions.

task: Develop and apply annotation schemes for labeling linguistic phenomena such as part-of-speech, named entities, or discourse relations.
substep: Assemble a representative sample of text to annotate, pulling a few hundred sentences from the target corpus that cover the genres and phenomena we expect (news, dialogue, historical text).

task: Develop and apply annotation schemes for labeling linguistic phenomena such as part-of-speech, named entities, or discourse relations.
substep: Draft the initial annotation guidelines: define each label, specify the annotation span/unit (token, mention, argument span), and write decision rules with positive and negative examples.

task: Develop and apply annotation schemes for labeling linguistic phenomena such as part-of-speech, named entities, or discourse relations.
substep: Run a small pilot annotation round with 2-3 annotators independently labeling the same 50-100 sentences using a tool like INCEpTION, brat, or Prodigy.

task: Develop and apply annotation schemes for labeling linguistic phenomena such as part-of-speech, named entities, or discourse relations.
substep: Compute inter-annotator agreement on the pilot data, using Cohen's/Fleiss' kappa for POS and NER labels and Krippendorff's alpha for span-based discourse relations.

task: Develop and apply annotation schemes for labeling linguistic phenomena such as part-of-speech, named entities, or discourse relations.
substep: Adjudicate disagreements in a reconciliation meeting, examining confusion matrices and borderline cases to find where the guidelines are ambiguous or the tagset is under- or over-specified.

task: Develop and apply annotation schemes for labeling linguistic phenomena such as part-of-speech, named entities, or discourse relations.
substep: Revise the guidelines and label set based on the disagreement analysis: merge or split labels, add clarifying rules for edge cases, and add a glossary of hard examples.

task: Develop and apply annotation schemes for labeling linguistic phenomena such as part-of-speech, named entities, or discourse relations.
substep: Iterate the pilot-agreement-revision loop until IAA stabilizes above an acceptable threshold (e.g. kappa > 0.8) and the guidelines are frozen.

task: Develop and apply annotation schemes for labeling linguistic phenomena such as part-of-speech, named entities, or discourse relations.
substep: Configure the annotation project for the full corpus: define annotation schema in the tool, set up double annotation with a curation layer, and assign batches to trained annotators.

task: Develop and apply annotation schemes for labeling linguistic phenomena such as part-of-speech, named entities, or discourse relations.
substep: Carry out full-scale annotation, monitoring throughput and running periodic spot-checks and calibration rounds to prevent annotator drift.

task: Develop and apply annotation schemes for labeling linguistic phenomena such as part-of-speech, named entities, or discourse relations.
substep: Curate and adjudicate the final gold standard, merging double-annotated files, resolving remaining conflicts, and producing a single authoritative labeled dataset.

task: Develop and apply annotation schemes for labeling linguistic phenomena such as part-of-speech, named entities, or discourse relations.
substep: Export the annotations to a standard interchange format (CoNLL-U for POS, CoNLL-2003/IOB for NER, or PDTB pipe-delimited for discourse) and validate schema consistency with format-checking scripts.

task: Develop and apply annotation schemes for labeling linguistic phenomena such as part-of-speech, named entities, or discourse relations.
substep: Document and release the scheme: publish the final guidelines, IAA statistics, label distributions, and a datasheet describing corpus provenance and annotation decisions.

task: Evaluate existing notation systems or language resources for how well they serve their intended use
substep: Specify the intended use case and target user community for the resource (e.g., IPA transcription for phonetic fieldwork, a treebank annotation scheme for parser training, or a WordNet-style lexical database for word-sense disambiguation), and write down the functional requirements it must satisfy.

task: Evaluate existing notation systems or language resources for how well they serve their intended use
substep: Gather the resource's documentation, schema definitions, annotation guidelines, and any published papers describing its design decisions and coverage claims.

task: Evaluate existing notation systems or language resources for how well they serve their intended use
substep: Assemble a representative sample of the data or notation instances, deliberately including hard cases (e.g., code-switching, tonal contrasts, non-projective dependencies, multiword expressions) that stress the system's expressive capacity.

task: Evaluate existing notation systems or language resources for how well they serve their intended use
substep: Define concrete evaluation criteria and metrics per requirement: coverage/recall against a gold list of phenomena, notational unambiguity, inter-annotator agreement (Cohen's/Fleiss' kappa), machine-readability, interoperability with standard formats (CoNLL-U, ISO 24617, Unicode/IPA), and completeness of the character/tag inventory.

task: Evaluate existing notation systems or language resources for how well they serve their intended use
substep: Attempt to encode the stress-test sample in the notation system by hand or with a conversion script, logging every case where the scheme forces an ambiguous, lossy, or impossible representation.

task: Evaluate existing notation systems or language resources for how well they serve their intended use
substep: Run a small reliability study: have two or more trained annotators apply the notation to the same sample and compute agreement, then adjudicate disagreements to distinguish annotator error from genuine underspecification in the guidelines.

task: Evaluate existing notation systems or language resources for how well they serve their intended use
substep: Check technical interoperability by loading the resource into the tools it is meant to feed (e.g., a parser, an ASR pipeline, a search interface, ELAN/Praat, or a UD validator) and record encoding errors, character normalization issues, and schema-validation failures.

task: Evaluate existing notation systems or language resources for how well they serve their intended use
substep: Compare the resource against one or two alternative notation systems or resources covering the same domain to benchmark relative coverage, granularity, and ease of use.

task: Evaluate existing notation systems or language resources for how well they serve their intended use
substep: Quantify and categorize the failure cases from S5-S8 into recurring gap types (missing inventory items, systematic ambiguity, cross-linguistic bias, tooling incompatibility) and estimate how frequently each occurs in realistic data.

task: Evaluate existing notation systems or language resources for how well they serve their intended use
substep: Score the resource against each criterion from S4, weight the criteria by their importance to the intended use case, and produce an overall fitness-for-purpose judgment.

task: Evaluate existing notation systems or language resources for how well they serve their intended use
substep: Write up the evaluation report with concrete evidence (example encodings, agreement figures, error tables) and actionable recommendations for extending, adapting, or replacing the resource for the intended use.

task: Code semantic shifts and grammatical changes in diachronic text corpora to track patterns of language evolution.
substep: Define the target linguistic variable(s) to be tracked (e.g., a modal verb undergoing grammaticalization, or a lexeme suspected of semantic broadening), and frame this within an explicit theory of change such as grammaticalization or subjectification to set coding categories.

task: Code semantic shifts and grammatical changes in diachronic text corpora to track patterns of language evolution.
substep: Assemble a chronologically-stratified corpus of the language (e.g., successive periods of the Penn Historical Corpora or the Corpus of Historical American English), dividing it into time bins and recording token counts per period for later normalization.

task: Code semantic shifts and grammatical changes in diachronic text corpora to track patterns of language evolution.
substep: Transcribe and normalize the historical/dialectal source texts, regularizing variant spellings and word boundaries so that the target forms can be searched consistently across periods.

task: Code semantic shifts and grammatical changes in diachronic text corpora to track patterns of language evolution.
substep: Extract all attestations of the target form(s) using KWIC concordancing (e.g., in AntConc or CQP), pulling each hit with enough surrounding context to judge its function and meaning.

task: Code semantic shifts and grammatical changes in diachronic text corpora to track patterns of language evolution.
substep: Add morphosyntactic annotation to each concordance line — POS, argument structure, syntactic slot, collocates — so grammatical behavior can be compared across time.

task: Code semantic shifts and grammatical changes in diachronic text corpora to track patterns of language evolution.
substep: Develop a coding scheme: define discrete codes for each semantic sense (e.g., spatial vs. temporal vs. epistemic reading) and each grammatical status (e.g., lexical verb vs. auxiliary vs. clitic), with operational criteria and diagnostic tests for assigning them.

task: Code semantic shifts and grammatical changes in diachronic text corpora to track patterns of language evolution.
substep: Manually code each attestation for sense and grammatical status by reading the context, applying the diagnostics, and flagging ambiguous or transitional tokens for a second pass.

task: Code semantic shifts and grammatical changes in diachronic text corpora to track patterns of language evolution.
substep: Check coding reliability by having a second annotator independently code a sample and computing inter-annotator agreement (e.g., Cohen's kappa), then reconcile disagreements and refine the coding manual.

task: Code semantic shifts and grammatical changes in diachronic text corpora to track patterns of language evolution.
substep: Screen the coded tokens for borrowings and calques that could mimic internal change, so that apparent shifts are not confounded with contact-induced innovation.

task: Code semantic shifts and grammatical changes in diachronic text corpora to track patterns of language evolution.
substep: Tabulate the coded categories by time bin, normalize frequencies per period size, and plot the trajectories to visualize the rise/decline of senses and grammatical functions over time.

task: Code semantic shifts and grammatical changes in diachronic text corpora to track patterns of language evolution.
substep: Test for significant diachronic trends (e.g., logistic regression or variability-based neighbor clustering on the coded proportions) to determine whether the shifts follow expected S-curve patterns of change.

task: Code semantic shifts and grammatical changes in diachronic text corpora to track patterns of language evolution.
substep: Interpret the coded patterns against grammaticalization/semantic-change theory, documenting the inferred pathway (e.g., concrete > abstract, verb > auxiliary) and noting the temporal window over which the change is reliably attested.

task: Review and synthesize the relevant literature to situate a research question within existing knowledge.
substep: Define the scope by identifying the relevant linguistic subfield(s) (e.g., phonology, syntax, sociolinguistics, historical linguistics, psycholinguistics) and the specific phenomenon, language, or language family under investigation, plus the theoretical framework(s) at stake (e.g., Minimalism, Optimality Theory, usage-based, variationist).

task: Review and synthesize the relevant literature to situate a research question within existing knowledge.
substep: Search discipline-specific databases and repositories: MLA International Bibliography, LLBA (Linguistics and Language Behavior Abstracts), the LINGUIST List, Google Scholar, Semantic Scholar, and for formal linguistics the open-access repositories lingbuzz and the Rutgers Optimality Archive; also glottolog and WALS for typological/areal grounding.

task: Review and synthesize the relevant literature to situate a research question within existing knowledge.
substep: Assemble foundational and canonical sources by tracing citation chains backward (reference lists of key papers) and forward (who cites the seminal work), including classic monographs, handbook chapters (e.g., Blackwell/Oxford/Cambridge handbooks), and grammars for the target language.

task: Review and synthesize the relevant literature to situate a research question within existing knowledge.
substep: Gather primary language data and descriptive resources cited in the literature: reference grammars, dictionaries, annotated corpora (e.g., BNC, COCA, CHILDES, Universal Dependencies treebanks), and archived fieldwork data, to check how empirical claims are supported.

task: Review and synthesize the relevant literature to situate a research question within existing knowledge.
substep: Read critically, evaluating each source for the strength of its empirical evidence (elicited judgments, corpus counts, experimental results), the adequacy of its data (native-speaker intuitions, sample size, cross-linguistic coverage), and its theoretical assumptions and analytical commitments.

task: Review and synthesize the relevant literature to situate a research question within existing knowledge.
substep: Organize the literature using a reference manager (Zotero, Mendeley, or BibTeX/BibLaTeX for LaTeX workflows), tagging works by phenomenon, language, framework, and type of evidence, and maintaining annotated notes on each source's key claims and analyses.

task: Review and synthesize the relevant literature to situate a research question within existing knowledge.
substep: Reconstruct the theoretical debate by mapping competing analyses and schools of thought, noting points of consensus, unresolved controversies, and how proposals differ in their treatment of the same data (e.g., movement vs. base-generation accounts).

task: Review and synthesize the relevant literature to situate a research question within existing knowledge.
substep: Synthesize cross-linguistic and typological generalizations, comparing how the phenomenon is described across languages and framing the target language's behavior against established universals, implicational hierarchies, or areal patterns.

task: Review and synthesize the relevant literature to situate a research question within existing knowledge.
substep: Write a coherent narrative literature review that connects prior findings to the research question, situating the study within a specific theoretical tradition and clarifying which prior claims or analyses it builds on, tests, or challenges (using the field's conventions, typically APA/Unified Style Sheet for Linguistics).

task: Acquire or access primary data sources relevant to research questions.
substep: Identify which type of primary data the research question requires: naturalistic speech/text, elicited data, experimental responses, or existing archival material, and whether it must cover a specific language, variety, register, or time period.

task: Acquire or access primary data sources relevant to research questions.
substep: Locate and access existing corpora and databases relevant to the language(s) of study, e.g., BNC, COCA, COHA, the CHILDES/TalkBank child-language archive, Universal Dependencies treebanks, WALS/Glottolog/PHOIBLE typological databases, or web/social-media corpora (Common Crawl, Twitter/X APIs).

task: Acquire or access primary data sources relevant to research questions.
substep: Consult and obtain materials from language archives and repositories for documented and endangered languages, e.g., ELAR, PARADISEC, AILLA, or the DoBeS/DOBES archive, negotiating access permissions and depositor restrictions.

task: Acquire or access primary data sources relevant to research questions.
substep: For fieldwork-based research, contact speech communities, recruit native-speaker consultants, and arrange sessions for recording naturalistic discourse or conducting targeted elicitation using stimuli (e.g., the Max Planck 'Frog Story', picture-naming sets, translation prompts).

task: Acquire or access primary data sources relevant to research questions.
substep: Record audio and video data in the field or lab using appropriate equipment (Zoom/Marantz recorders, head-mounted microphones, video cameras) and phonetic/instrumental tools such as electroglottography, ultrasound, or Praat-compatible acquisition setups for phonetic studies.

task: Acquire or access primary data sources relevant to research questions.
substep: Collect experimental/behavioral data through psycholinguistic paradigms (self-paced reading, eye-tracking, ERP, acceptability-judgment or rating tasks) deployed via platforms like PCIbex, Gorilla, E-Prime, or hosted on crowdsourcing services (Prolific, Amazon Mechanical Turk).

task: Acquire or access primary data sources relevant to research questions.
substep: Assemble historical and philological primary sources by consulting manuscript collections, digitized text editions, historical corpora, epigraphic databases, and dictionaries/etymological references for diachronic and historical-linguistic questions.

task: Acquire or access primary data sources relevant to research questions.
substep: Build a custom corpus when no suitable resource exists: scrape or download texts, transcribe recordings (in ELAN, Transcriber, or Praat TextGrids), and compile the material into a searchable, metadata-tagged dataset.

task: Acquire or access primary data sources relevant to research questions.
substep: Secure legal and licensing clearance for data use, including copyright, corpus end-user license agreements, data-access agreements, and community/consultant permissions governing sensitive or restricted materials.

task: Acquire or access primary data sources relevant to research questions.
substep: Verify that acquired data has adequate coverage, quality, and representativeness for the research question (sufficient tokens/speakers, balanced across relevant variables) and supplement or re-collect if gaps are found.

task: Design, build, and iteratively refine artifacts such as devices, software, materials, systems, or creative works to meet specified requirements.
substep: Specify the artifact's requirements and scope: e.g., define the target languages/varieties, annotation categories, coverage, and intended users for a corpus, lexicon, treebank, grammar checker, or NLP tool.

task: Design, build, and iteratively refine artifacts such as devices, software, materials, systems, or creative works to meet specified requirements.
substep: Design an annotation scheme or data model, drawing on established standards (e.g., Universal Dependencies, Leipzig Glossing Rules, TEI/XML, ELAN tiers, IPA conventions, ISO 24617 for annotation).

task: Design, build, and iteratively refine artifacts such as devices, software, materials, systems, or creative works to meet specified requirements.
substep: Build the underlying resource: transcribe and time-align speech/signs (Praat, ELAN, FLEx), compile and mark up texts, or encode a grammar formalism (LFG/XLE, HPSG, finite-state morphology with foma/xfst).

task: Design, build, and iteratively refine artifacts such as devices, software, materials, systems, or creative works to meet specified requirements.
substep: Implement software components: write scripts or models (Python with NLTK/spaCy, R, regex, XSLT) to tokenize, parse, tag, or train language models on the annotated data.

task: Design, build, and iteratively refine artifacts such as devices, software, materials, systems, or creative works to meet specified requirements.
substep: Author annotation/coding guidelines and train annotators or coders so that the artifact is produced consistently across contributors.

task: Design, build, and iteratively refine artifacts such as devices, software, materials, systems, or creative works to meet specified requirements.
substep: Pilot-test the artifact on a sample and measure inter-annotator agreement (Cohen's/Fleiss' kappa) or system performance (precision/recall/F1, WER, parse accuracy) against gold-standard data.

task: Design, build, and iteratively refine artifacts such as devices, software, materials, systems, or creative works to meet specified requirements.
substep: Diagnose errors and edge cases by inspecting misannotations, unhandled linguistic phenomena (e.g., code-switching, dialectal forms, rare constructions), and coverage gaps.

task: Design, build, and iteratively refine artifacts such as devices, software, materials, systems, or creative works to meet specified requirements.
substep: Iteratively refine the scheme, rules, or model — revising guidelines, adding lexical entries or grammar rules, retraining, and re-evaluating until the resource meets validity and reliability targets.

task: Design, build, and iteratively refine artifacts such as devices, software, materials, systems, or creative works to meet specified requirements.
substep: Validate the artifact against native-speaker judgments, external corpora, or expert review to confirm linguistic adequacy and descriptive accuracy.

task: Design, build, and iteratively refine artifacts such as devices, software, materials, systems, or creative works to meet specified requirements.
substep: Document the artifact (metadata, versioning, README, data statements) and package it for archiving and sharing in repositories (e.g., TROLLing, LDC, CLARIN, OLAC, GitHub) following FAIR principles.
